opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think a lot of it comes down to the same thing that's driven progress all along: the models just need to get smarter. When people talk about agent reliability, they often frame it as a separate engineering problem, as if we need some clever scaffolding or orchestration layer on top. Those things help, but the core issue is that if each step in a long chain has even a small chance of going wrong, those errors compound. If you're doing a task with fifty steps and you're 95% reliable at each one, you're going to fail most of the time.

So you need two things. One is raw capability: better reasoning, better judgment about what to do next, so the per-step error rate drops a lot. The other, maybe even more important, is the ability to notice when you've made a mistake and recover from it. Humans aren't perfectly reliable either. We make errors constantly, but we catch them. We look at the result, realize it doesn't make sense, and back up. Getting models to do that self-checking well, knowing when they're uncertain, when to verify, when to ask for help, is a big part of making agents actually usable.

There's also the question of compute at inference time. We've seen that letting models think longer, try multiple approaches, and check their work makes a big difference. For agents doing high-stakes or complex work, it makes sense to spend a lot more compute per task, because the value of getting it right is high. That's a lever we're only starting to pull.

And then there's trust. For widespread use, people need to be able to hand off a task and not babysit it. That means the system has to be predictable and transparent enough that you understand what it did and why. I think we'll get there step by step: first agents doing things where mistakes are cheap and easy to check, then gradually more autonomy as the track record builds. It's a lot like how you'd treat a new employee.

But fundamentally, I'm optimistic. The trend lines on capability are steep, and a lot of what looks like a reliability problem today is going to look like a capability problem we solved a year or two from now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses improving capability, self-checking, and inference-time compute, but does not say agent control problems require general solutions.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare users and developers or say users are better at discovering agent use cases.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: You know, I think a lot of what people call the "agent problem" is really just a model quality problem wearing a different hat. When I look at where agents fall down today, it's rarely some exotic failure in the orchestration layer. It's that the model makes a dumb mistake on step seven of a thirty-step task, and then everything downstream of that is built on sand. Humans do this too, but we have this nice property where we notice we've gone off the rails and back up. Models are getting better at that, but they're still too confident when they're wrong.

So the first thing is just, the models need to be smarter and more calibrated, and I don't think that's a cop-out answer. Every time the base model gets substantially better, a whole class of scaffolding that people built to compensate for its weaknesses just evaporates. I've seen that happen over and over. People spend six months building clever retry logic and verification loops, and then the next model comes out and doesn't need it.

But there's a second piece that I think is more interesting, which is around what the model is actually optimized for. Right now we mostly train these things to produce a good answer in a single shot, or in a short exchange. An agent that's going to run for hours, touching real systems, needs a different disposition. It needs to be the kind of entity that pauses before doing something irreversible, that asks for help when the situation is genuinely ambiguous, that keeps track of what it's already tried. Those aren't really intelligence in the raw sense. They're more like temperament, and we're only beginning to learn how to train for temperament.

And then the third thing, honestly, is boring engineering. Reliability at scale is a systems problem. You want these agents to be cheap enough to run many times and check themselves, fast enough that a human can stay in the loop without falling asleep, and you want the failure modes to be legible. When something goes wrong, you should be able to look at the trace and understand why. A lot of the compute work I've spent my life on is really in service of that: making the thing cheap and fast enough that you can afford to be careful with it.

If I had to bet, I'd say we're in a period where it looks like agents need enormous amounts of special-purpose infrastructure, and in five years a lot of that will look like the training wheels it was. But the piece about getting the model to want to behave well over long horizons, to be a good colleague rather than a brilliant intern who never asks questions, that's going to be real and durable work.

r001.rationale: It describes improving model quality, training for long-horizon behavior, and engineering reliability, but does not state that agent control problems require general solutions.

astra-6.text:
I think the big thing is being able to do longer tasks reliably. If you have a system that gets each step right 99 percent of the time, that sounds pretty good. But if the task takes a thousand steps, you’re going to have problems. And the steps aren’t independent—one mistake can change everything that follows.

So you need more than better answers. You need the system to check its work, notice when something has gone wrong, and recover. It needs to be able to run a test, look at the result, and change its approach. And it needs some judgment about when to ask the user a question instead of continuing with a bad assumption.

I’d expect progress to come from both smarter models and better systems around them. You want to give agents useful tools and ways to verify success. Then you can let them work on increasingly long tasks as they demonstrate that they can actually finish them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reliability, checking, recovery, tools, and verification, but does not state that agent control problems likely require general solutions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big thing is getting them to do longer tasks reliably. Being right 95 percent of the time on an individual step sounds pretty good, but if you need a hundred steps to accomplish something, that’s a problem. You need the system to notice when it’s made a mistake, check its work, and recover.

Some of that comes from making the underlying models smarter. Some comes from giving them tools and training them to use those tools well. If you can run the code, inspect the result, and fix it, you don’t have to get everything right on the first try.

And they need to be better at figuring out when to ask a person. You don’t want an agent asking permission for every little thing, but you also don’t want it confidently making an expensive mistake. I think getting that balance right, and learning from tasks where you can actually measure whether the job got done, will be a big part of making these systems useful.
